title: ML: statistical evaluation
summary: Twelve executable studies of group/time splits, ranking metrics, calibration, confidence intervals, paired experiments, multiple comparisons, out-of-fold predictions and nested selection. Assumptions and failure cases accompany the arithmetic.

lessons.title: Split identities before splitting examples
lessons.body:
# Split identities before splitting examples

Randomly splitting rows leaks information when several rows belong to the same person, device or document. Validation must separate the unit that will actually be new at deployment. Keeping a group intact can produce uneven fold sizes; equal row counts are less important than avoiding leakage.

This deterministic allocator sorts group names and assigns them round-robin to folds. It is a simple reproducible policy rather than an optimal balance algorithm. Evaluate whether labels and groups are confounded before interpreting a fold score. A grouped split cannot repair a target that already contains future information.

```python
groups=["a","a","b","c"]
assigned={g:i%2 for i,g in enumerate(sorted(set(groups)))}
print([assigned[g] for g in groups])
```

## Review the design

The split unit should match the deployment question. Group separation estimates new-group performance; it does not estimate future drift within groups, so a time-aware design may also be required.
lessons.task: Implement group_folds(groups,k) returning k lists of row indices. Sort distinct group names and assign group number modulo k. Require 2<=k<=number of distinct groups.

checks.name: identity never crosses folds

lessons.title: Purge a gap before a temporal validation window
lessons.body:
# Purge a gap before a temporal validation window

Future deployment requires validation in the future of the training data. Shuffling time series can teach a model from later observations and then evaluate it on earlier ones. A gap additionally separates training from the validation boundary when features or labels have a lookahead horizon.

This contract uses integer timestamps and an inclusive validation interval. Training observations must be strictly earlier than start minus gap. Choosing the gap requires knowledge of feature availability and label construction; an arbitrary gap is not proof that the pipeline is free of leakage.

```python
times=[1,2,3,4,5,6]
start,gap=5,1
print([i for i,t in enumerate(times) if t<start-gap])
```

## Review the design

A temporal split must be combined with point-in-time feature joins and train-only preprocessing. Time order alone does not prevent using a feature published after the prediction timestamp.

lessons.title: Treat tied ranking scores explicitly in ROC AUC
lessons.body:
# Treat tied ranking scores explicitly in ROC AUC

ROC AUC is the probability that a randomly selected positive example receives a higher score than a negative example, with half credit for a tie. This interpretation yields a small exact reference implementation that is useful for testing a faster ranking implementation.

AUC evaluates ranking, not probability calibration or the cost of one operating threshold. With no positive or no negative examples the pairwise probability is undefined. Returning zero would confuse an impossible evaluation with a perfectly reversed ranking. Report the population and class counts alongside the metric.

```python
positive=[.8,.5]
negative=[.5,.1]
credits=[(p>n)+.5*(p==n) for p in positive for n in negative]
print(sum(credits)/len(credits))
```

## Review the design

The quadratic reference is transparent for tiny evaluation fixtures. Large datasets should use a tie-aware rank algorithm. A high AUC can coexist with poor calibration or unacceptable errors at the chosen threshold.
lessons.task: Implement roc_auc(labels,scores) for equal nonempty lists, binary integer labels and finite scores. Compute exact positive-negative pair credit, half for ties. Reject single-class data.

checks.name: undefined or invalid rankings fail

hints: Separate scores by true label, then compare every positive-negative pair.
Do not use >= for a full point on tied scores.

The quadratic reference is transparent for tiny evaluation fixtures. Large datasets should use a tie-aware rank algorithm. A high AUC can coexist with poor calibration or unacceptable errors at the chosen threshold.
lessons.explanation: The quadratic reference is transparent for tiny evaluation fixtures. Large datasets should use a tie-aware rank algorithm. A high AUC can coexist with poor calibration or unacceptable errors at the chosen threshold.

lessons.title: Compute average precision at tied score boundaries
lessons.body:
# Compute average precision at tied score boundaries

Precision-recall metrics expose failure under class imbalance that accuracy can hide. Average precision weights each precision value by the increase in recall at a score threshold. It is not the trapezoidal area obtained by linearly interpolating precision between thresholds.

Rows with equal scores must enter together. Breaking ties by input order can produce different metrics for the same model predictions. The contract returns zero for no positive labels, a deliberate reporting convention that should accompany the metric. It rejects invalid labels and mismatched lengths rather than silently truncating pairs.

```python
labels=[1,0,1]
precision_at_positive=[1,2/3]
print(sum(precision_at_positive)/sum(labels))
```

## Review the design

Average precision depends on prevalence and the evaluation population. Compare models on the same test population and retain class counts; a number alone does not establish business value.
lessons.task: Implement average_precision(labels,scores). Group equal scores descending, accumulate TP and seen count, and sum (new positives/total positives)*precision at each group. Return 0 with no positives; validate nonempty equal lengths, binary labels and finite scores.

checks.name: precision is weighted by recall increments
ties are invariant to row order

hints: Accumulate all labels at one score before measuring its precision.

lessons.title: Measure probability error instead of only decisions
lessons.body:
# Measure probability error instead of only decisions

Two classifiers can make identical binary decisions while assigning very different probabilities. Brier score measures the mean squared difference between each predicted positive probability and its binary outcome. It is sensitive to probability quality, while thresholded accuracy discards that information.

The score alone does not separate reliability, resolution and label uncertainty. Compare it with a prevalence baseline and inspect calibration across useful slices. Validate probabilities before calculating: clipping an invalid model output would hide a broken probability contract and make a metric look better than the actual system behavior.

```python
labels=[1,0]
probabilities=[.8,.2]
print(sum((p-y)**2 for y,p in zip(labels,probabilities))/2)
```

## Review the design

A proper scoring rule rewards truthful probabilities in expectation, but finite test scores still have uncertainty. Use held-out calibration data and avoid choosing a calibrator on the final test set.
lessons.task: Implement brier(labels,probabilities), validating equal nonempty sequences, binary integer labels and finite probabilities in [0,1]. Return mean squared probability error.
lessons.solution:
import math
def brier(labels,probabilities):
    if not labels or len(labels)!=len(probabilities) or any(type(y) is not int or y not in (0,1) for y in labels) or any(not math.isfinite(p) or not 0<=p<=1 for p in probabilities):raise ValueError('invalid probabilities')
    squared_errors=[(p-y)**2 for y,p in zip(labels,probabilities)]
    total_error=sum(squared_errors)
    result=total_error/len(labels)
    return result

checks.name: rejects hidden clipping and truncation

hints: Square each probability error, then average over observations.
Validate before arithmetic; zip by itself hides mismatched lengths.

A proper scoring rule rewards truthful probabilities in expectation, but finite test scores still have uncertainty. Use held-out calibration data and avoid choosing a calibrator on the final test set.
lessons.explanation: A proper scoring rule rewards truthful probabilities in expectation, but finite test scores still have uncertainty. Use held-out calibration data and avoid choosing a calibrator on the final test set.

lessons.title: Estimate calibration with explicit bin semantics
lessons.body:
# Estimate calibration with explicit bin semantics

A calibration diagram compares average confidence with observed frequency. Expected calibration error summarizes absolute gaps weighted by bin occupancy. The binning rule is part of the metric: changing the bin count can change the score without changing the model.

The final bin must include probability one. Empty bins contribute no weight and should not invent an observed frequency. ECE is a diagnostic, not a universal proper scoring rule; a small value on coarse bins can conceal substantial errors. Keep Brier score or log loss and examine subgroup reliability as well.

```python
probabilities=[.1,.9,1.0]
print([min(int(p*2),1) for p in probabilities])
```

## Review the design

ECE depends on discretization and sample size. Treat it as an inspectable diagnostic rather than a calibrated confidence interval or a substitute for a proper scoring rule.
lessons.task: Implement ece(labels,probs,bins) using equal-width bins [i/bins,(i+1)/bins), with 1 in the last. Validate binary labels, finite [0,1] probabilities, equal nonempty lengths and positive integer bins.

checks.name: rejects invalid bins and probabilities

hints: Collect observations by their probability bin, clamping only the valid endpoint 1.
The weighted gap is abs(sum probabilities - sum outcomes)/total count per occupied bin.
ECE depends on discretization and sample size. Treat it as an inspectable diagnostic rather than a calibrated confidence interval or a substitute for a proper scoring rule.
lessons.explanation: ECE depends on discretization and sample size. Treat it as an inspectable diagnostic rather than a calibrated confidence interval or a substitute for a proper scoring rule.

lessons.title: Report uncertainty for a measured success rate
lessons.body:
# Report uncertainty for a measured success rate

A success rate from ten examples should not carry the same confidence as one from ten thousand. A Wilson interval adjusts a binomial proportion using the sample count and a chosen normal quantile. Unlike a naive symmetric interval, it behaves sensibly near zero and one.

The calculation assumes independent Bernoulli observations. Correlated sessions or repeated users violate that simple sampling model; resample at the independent group level instead. The exercise accepts z explicitly so the confidence convention is visible and testable. An interval describes sampling uncertainty under assumptions, not protection from dataset bias.

```python
import math
n=10;p=.5;z=1.96
den=1+z*z/n
center=(p+z*z/(2*n))/den
half=z*math.sqrt(p*(1-p)/n+z*z/(4*n*n))/den
print(round(center-half,3),round(center+half,3))
```

## Review the design

The z value determines the nominal confidence level through a normal approximation. Independence and representative sampling matter more than the number of decimals printed in the interval.
lessons.task: Implement wilson(successes,total,z=1.96) returning lower,upper. Require integer 0<=successes<=total, total>0, and finite z>0. Clamp floating roundoff to [0,1].

checks.name: sample size matters and invalid inputs fail

hints: Use the Wilson center and denominator, not p plus or minus a naive standard error.
Keep successes and total validated as counts.
The z value determines the nominal confidence level through a normal approximation. Independence and representative sampling matter more than the number of decimals printed in the interval.
lessons.explanation: The z value determines the nominal confidence level through a normal approximation. Independence and representative sampling matter more than the number of decimals printed in the interval.

lessons.title: Resample paired model differences with a local RNG
lessons.body:
# Resample paired model differences with a local RNG

Two models evaluated on the same cases produce paired measurements. Resampling their scores independently discards that pairing and changes the uncertainty question. Resample case indices once per replicate and compute the mean of paired differences.

This exercise takes precomputed per-case differences, a local random seed and an explicit nearest-rank quantile rule. It does not modify the process-global random generator. The percentile bootstrap has limitations for small or dependent samples; user-level or time-block resampling is needed when rows are not independent. Fix the analysis plan before comparing many candidate models.

```python
import random
rng=random.Random(4)
differences=[1,-1,2]
print([rng.choice(differences) for _ in range(3)])
```

## Review the design

Pairing preserves the shared test cases. This interval is conditional on the chosen dataset and resampling assumptions; it does not account for selecting the best model after looking at many bootstrap intervals.
lessons.task: Implement bootstrap_interval(differences,repeats,seed,alpha=.05). Draw n indices with replacement for each replicate, sort replicate means, and return indices floor((alpha/2)*(repeats-1)) and ceil((1-alpha/2)*(repeats-1)). Require nonempty finite data, repeats>=2, and 0<alpha<1.

hints: Resample one index per case from a local Random instance.

lessons.title: Enumerate a tiny paired randomization test
lessons.body:
# Enumerate a tiny paired randomization test

A paired randomization test asks how surprising the observed mean difference would be if either model could exchange its outcome on each case. For a small independent paired sample, enumerate every sign assignment instead of relying on simulation.

The two-sided statistic uses the absolute mean, and ties count as at least as extreme. Exchangeability under the null is an assumption, not a property guaranteed by arithmetic. The exact enumerator is intentionally bounded to twelve cases because its cost doubles with each additional case. Large or dependent experiments need a different sampling and analysis design.

```python
import itertools
values=[1,2]
null=[sum(s*x for s,x in zip(signs,values)) for signs in itertools.product((-1,1),repeat=2)]
print(null)
```

## Review the design

Exact enumeration removes Monte Carlo error, not modeling assumptions. A small p-value does not measure effect size or the probability that a production release will improve user outcomes.
lessons.task: Implement sign_flip_p(differences) for 1..12 finite values. Enumerate all sign combinations and return the fraction with absolute summed difference >= the observed absolute sum, with 1e-12 tie tolerance.

checks.name: bounded computational contract

hints: Enumerate (-1,1) to the number of pairs.

Exact enumeration removes Monte Carlo error, not modeling assumptions. A small p-value does not measure effect size or the probability that a production release will improve user outcomes.

lessons.title: Adjust a family of discoveries without losing original order
lessons.body:
# Adjust a family of discoveries without losing original order

Trying many hypotheses and reporting only the smallest unadjusted p-value creates false discoveries. Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment controls the expected false-discovery proportion under its assumptions by considering the whole declared family.

Sort p-values, multiply by family size divided by rank, and apply a reverse cumulative minimum. Without that last step adjusted values can violate rank monotonicity. Return results in the original hypothesis order so decisions remain attached to the correct experiment. Selecting the family after inspecting results defeats the point of the adjustment.

```python
pvalues=[.01,.04,.03]
ranked=sorted(enumerate(pvalues),key=lambda x:x[1])
print(ranked)
```

## Review the design

BH controls a false-discovery rate under conditions such as independent or suitable positively dependent tests. It does not establish a causal effect or replace a predeclared experiment and a meaningful effect-size threshold.
lessons.task: Implement bh_adjust(pvalues) returning BH adjusted values in original order, capped at 1. Accept empty input. Reject nonfinite values or values outside [0,1].

checks.name: reverse minimum preserves rank constraints
checks.code: r=bh_adjust([.01,.04,.03]);assert all(abs(a-b)<1e-12 for a,b in zip(r,[.03,.04,.04]))

lessons.title: Reject overlapping or incomplete out-of-fold predictions
lessons.body:
# Reject overlapping or incomplete out-of-fold predictions

A stacking model needs predictions made without fitting the first-stage estimator on the same row. Out-of-fold construction can silently leak if a row appears in two held-out sets or if training predictions fill missing positions.

This exercise validates coverage while assembling predictions supplied by fold. It cannot inspect how each estimator was trained, so the fold-training contract remains a separate responsibility. Preserve row identity explicitly and reject duplicates instead of averaging them away. A complete audit retains each fold's training and validation identities and the preprocessing state fitted on its training partition.

```python
predictions=[None]*3
for index,value in [(2,.8),(0,.1),(1,.4)]:
    predictions[index]=value
print(predictions)
```

## Review the design

Complete nonoverlapping assembly is necessary but not sufficient for honest out-of-fold prediction. The training procedure and feature transformations must also exclude each held-out row and its leakage group.
lessons.task: Implement assemble_oof(n,folds) where folds contain (indices,predictions). Require each index in range(n) exactly once and equal lengths per fold; return predictions in row order. Reject missing or duplicate indices.

lessons.title: Select inside each outer evaluation fold
lessons.body:
# Select inside each outer evaluation fold

The score used to choose a hyperparameter is optimistically biased as a performance estimate. Nested evaluation separates inner selection from outer assessment. Each outer fold chooses its own candidate using only its inner validation scores, then evaluates that choice on the untouched outer partition.

This exercise receives precomputed scores so selection leakage can be tested without a costly training run. Candidate names break exact ties deterministically. The outer result is consulted only after selection; choosing a candidate by its outer score is explicitly the bug the checks expose.

```python
inner={"small":[.7,.8],"large":[.9,.5]}
chosen=min(inner,key=lambda k:(-sum(inner[k])/len(inner[k]),k))
print(chosen)
```

## Review the design

Nested evaluation estimates the full selection procedure rather than one fixed configuration. Final deployment still needs a separately chosen configuration, a locked test set when appropriate, and an uncertainty analysis.
lessons.task: Implement nested_report(folds). Each fold is a dict candidate -> {inner:[scores], outer:score}. Select highest mean inner score, lexical name on ties. Return (chosen_names,mean selected outer score). Validate nonempty folds/candidates/inner scores and finite numbers.

checks.name: outer score cannot select the winner
selection is per fold with stable ties
invalid experiments fail

hints: Choose a candidate from inner scores before reading its outer result.
Use a separate selection for every outer fold, then aggregate held-out scores.

Nested evaluation estimates the full selection procedure rather than one fixed configuration. Final deployment still needs a separately chosen configuration, a locked test set when appropriate, and an uncertainty analysis.
lessons.explanation: Nested evaluation estimates the full selection procedure rather than one fixed configuration. Final deployment still needs a separately chosen configuration, a locked test set when appropriate, and an uncertainty analysis.
